newsitem.title: UK: Euro bourses mixed, London defies continent.
newsitem.headline: Euro bourses mixed, London defies continent.

text.p: A mixed opening on Wall Street provided little impetus to European shares on Thursday, with continental bourses holding to their earlier losses while London continued to prove buoyant.

On the currency markets, tough yen-supportive rhetoric from two key Japanese Ministry of Finance (MOF) officials pushed the dollar from its 55-month peak against the yen, although it managed to reclaim some lost ground.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said in a television interview that a strong currency was in U.S. interests and that the country's dollar policy was "absolutely unchanged".

The U.S. currency also edged lower against the mark despite German officials breaking their conspicuous silent of the last few days with remarks that they were comfortable with the dollar's high level.
Wall Street's overnight drop of 0.69 percent drove continental share markets lower at their open and they continued to face pressure.

By late afternoon German shares were down 0.24 percent while the Paris bourse doubled its earlier losses to 0.65 percent. London also took an early dip in line with Wall Street, but recovered modestly, with the FTSE-100 index up 13.1 points, or 0.31 percent, at 4,305.4 points late in the session.

Strong demand for utility and drug stocks helped drive the gains in London. Investors turned to utilities after press reports suggested that the opposition Labour Party's planned windfall tax on privatised utilities would be lower than some expected.
Labour's finance spokesman, Gordon Brown, said a decision on the size of the one-off tax would not be made until after Britain's May 1 general election.
Drugs stocks rose after promising trial results on a new drug for treating Hepatitis B raised hope that pharmaceuticals giant Glaxo Wellcome may have a blockbuster drug on its hands.
Finance minister Kenneth Clarke began his last monthly meeting on monetary policy before the election with Bank of England Governor Eddie George at 1425 GMT.
Analysts believe an unpopular interest rate rise, which many think needed to nip inflation, would come after the polls rather than before, whoever wins.
"No one really expects an interest rate rise but no one can afford to be disinterested just in case," said one dealer.
Paris dealers had hoped that the Bank of France might trim interest rates on Thursday. But the central bank left rates unchanged and the market consolidated after Wednesday's gains.
The CAC-40 index was down 17.01 points, or 0.65 percent, to 2,600.54 by the late afternoon.

Wall Street also pulled down the German market, with the DAX index closing down 7.97 points or 0.24 percent at 3,351.49. The IBIS index, which measures electronic trading, later fell further and was down 13.16 points at 3,351.60.

Dealers also blamed the weakening of the dollar against the mark. German industry has benefited from the mark's weakness in recent months against the dollar and sterling, which has tracked the U.S. currency more than its European counterparts.

In one of the most explicit warnings yet about the dollar's sharp rise against the yen, Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said that recent yen moves were "obviously excessive" and cautioned that such moves would be dealt with decisively and in a timely matter.

Eisuke Sakakibara, head of the ministry's International Finance Bureau, also called recent dollar/yen movements "too rapid" and warned that intervention was possible if foreign exchange rates deviated from fundamentals.
Following the stern warning about an overly weak yen, the dollar fell to 126.00 yen compared with the high of 127.16 in Asia and Wednesday's European close of 126.83.

"The comments from the MOF are clearly drawing a line in the sand, which is unnerving simply because the dollar has risen so far so sharply," said Mark Hendriks, international economist at SBC Warburg in London.
After its early slide, the dollar rebounded against the mark to 1.7162 compared with the previous close of 1.7250, although well off its earlier 37-month high of 1.7272 marks.

This followed comments from Bundesbank Council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher, who said: "We do not need to strengthen the mark." The state secretary at the German finance ministry, Juergen Stark, also said a dollar/mark exchange rate over 1.72 was part of a normal market correction.
CURRENCIES AT 1400 GMT
The dollar was quoted around 1.7162 marks and 126.00 yen, compared with 1.7250 and 126.83 in late European trade on Wednesday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1400 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was up 13.1 points at 4,305.4.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index closed down 7.97 points at 3,351.49.
PARIS - The CAC-40 index was 17.01 points lower at 2,600.54.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed in the afternoon at $347.60 an ounce after a morning fixing at $348.05 and compared with the London close of $347.95 on Wednesday. Silver was down one cent at $4.78.
